title: F1 manufacturers to vote on mid-season rule change in engine row
content:
SAKHIR, Bahrain — Formula 1’s engine manufacturers will vote next week on a mid-season rule change addressing the compression ratio row that has centered on Mercedes.

Over the winter, it emerged that Mercedes had found a potential advantage with its new engine for the 2026 season relating to the compression ratio limits. This relates to the amount of fuel the engine can squeeze before burning it as a way to produce more power.

While the F1 regulations set a limit of 16:1 and test the engines when cold in the garage, it was understood that Mercedes had managed to exceed that ratio and reached 18:1 when the engine was hot while still complying with the measurements at the required times.

Concerns about this potential advantage led to opposition from its rival manufacturers — Audi, Ferrari, Honda and Red Bull/Ford — who sought clarity from the FIA in recent weeks, as well as pushing for new tests to be introduced to ensure compliance even when active.

On Wednesday, the FIA issued a statement confirming that while there would be no rule changes before the new season, thus ending the risk of the results of the first race in Australia being protested, the rules could change mid-season.

A proposal has been put forward that, from Aug. 1, teams must display compliance with compression ratio limit not only in ambient conditions, but also when at an operating temperature of 130ºC.

“The vote has been submitted to the Power Unit Manufacturers, and its outcome is expected within the next 10 days and will be communicated in due course,” said the FIA statement.

“As with all Formula 1 regulatory changes, any amendment remains subject to final approval by the FIA World Motor Sport Council.”

Should the motion to introduce the new testing receive a ‘super majority’, which means the backing of five of the seven parties, then it would be pushed through and become part of F1’s regulations during the summer break.

Toto Wolff, the Mercedes team principal, told reporters earlier this month that he thought rival teams could be making excuses before the season had even started, and called on them to “get your s— together.” He also stated there were zero concerns about the legality of Mercedes’ engine, having received clarification and reassurances from the FIA.

Wolff then claimed last week in Bahrain that the possible advantage being discussed was only worth a couple of horsepower, and warned of “unknown consequences” of trying to force through a rule change before the start of the new season, especially with long lead times on developing the engines.

Prior to the FIA’s statement being issued, James Vowles, whose Williams team uses Mercedes engines, said in a news conference there was “probably a misunderstanding” of the extent of the advantage. He said the matter was “just noise, and noise frankly will go away.”

His counterpart at Red Bull, Laurent Mekies, disagreed, believing that any competitive advantage would make a difference this year.

“We don’t think it’s noise,” he said. “We simply think we must have the clarity. We are not stressed if it goes left or if it goes right. We must have the clarity on what we can and what we cannot do.”

Support for the motion seems likely should the four rival manufacturers stay united on the issue, given F1 and the FIA tend to go with the majority of teams.

Delaying the change in the testing until August would give Mercedes time to make any necessary adjustments to its power units, which it supplies to McLaren, Williams and Alpine in addition to its own F1 team.

But Wolff and Vowles had raised questions about the rationale of seeking changes due to concerns about a performance deficit, given Mercedes’ engineers had simply pushed the regulations to their limits while ensuring compliance.

“I think the very essence of Formula 1 is to find performance,” Wolff said last week. “(It’s) to attract the best engineers and the best people, give them freedom to develop regulations. One time it goes for you and another time it goes against you.”
